extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and pharmaceutical/chemical R&D and IP teams filing or prosecuting patents in India
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for evaluating and overcoming objections under Section 3(d) of the Indian Patents Act, with emphasis on chemical and pharmaceutical product and process claims. Explains statutory text, judicial interpretation (Novartis, Chugai), evidentiary expectations, and prosecution strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has to satisfy the conditions of Novelty, Inventive step, and Industrial Applicability in order to be patentable in India.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the baseline requirements; in addition to these, an invention must also not fall within the non-patentable subject matter listed under Section 3 of the Patents Act (including Section 3(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(d) barred categories (textual standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d) bars 'the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance or the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance or of the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation in the statute: 'salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations, and other derivatives of known substance shall be considered to be the same substance, unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.' Use this textual formulation as the primary statutory test when assessing patentability under Section 3(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivatives treated as same substance unless significant efficacy difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms such as salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives are considered the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties with regard to efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome a Section 3(d) objection for a derivative (e.g., salt, polymorph), the applicant must show that the derivative 'differs significantly in properties with regard to efficacy' compared to the known substance; mere physicochemical improvements not directly tied to efficacy may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy defined functionally (therapeutic efficacy for drugs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of 'efficacy' depends upon the function, utility or the purpose of the product under consideration; for drugs and medicines, 'therapeutic efficacy'—i.e., increased efficiency or ability to cure a particular disease—is the relevant measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Supreme Court (Novartis) holding: only properties directly relating to the product's function (for drugs, curing disease) count as 'efficacy'. Other advantageous properties are not automatically relevant unless they translate into improved therapeutic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard for enhanced efficacy (experimental/clinical data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enhanced/therapeutic efficacy must be validated by experimental data; mere demonstration of enhanced bioavailability is not sufficient unless it is specifically claimed and established that it leads to enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative data must directly show superior ability to treat a patient (e.g., improved clinical outcome). Data such as bioavailability, flowability, disintegration, dissolution, etc., may be insufficient in India unless connected causally and experimentally to improved therapeutic effect. The Novartis precedent requires research data linking the claimed property to therapeutic benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty determination as a way to avoid Section 3(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject matter is considered novel by the Controller (or is made novel by amendment/argument), it cannot be treated as a known process/substance under Section 3(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When novelty can be established, submit a detailed and persuasive reply on novelty and inventive step together with supportive arguments related to technical effects/advantages of the claim features to rebut Section 3(d) objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/method claims—'mere use' prohibition and escape routes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d) bars the 'mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus' unless such known process results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome Section 3(d) for process claims, either (a) claim a process that results in a new product, (b) show the process employs at least one new reactant, or (c) demonstrate a significant improvement over existing prior art (with supporting data) showing the claimed method is more than a mere use of known method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial application—Novartis precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Novartis AG v. Union of India: the Court held that for pharmaceutical inventions the test of efficacy is tied to function/utility (therapeutic efficacy), and that enhanced bioavailability alone is not sufficient to meet Section 3(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on Novartis when arguing what types of data and which endpoints are relevant: must specifically claim and establish that a claimed property increases therapeutic efficacy in treating disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial application—Chugai Seiyaku (tablet/process) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Delhi High Court in Chugai Seiyaku v. Controller (April 6, 2022) held that a method of producing a tablet of a pre-existing drug via direct compression was not patentable under Section 3(d) and lack of inventive step where prior art disclosed tablet forms and the improvement (e.g., disintegration/dissolution) did not establish enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine whether the claimed improvement has a demonstrated effect on treatment, the extent of improvement, whether prior art already discloses the form/product, and whether the claim is an attempt to 'evergreen' earlier patents. Superiority in formulation properties without showing clinical/therapeutic benefit is likely insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-evergreening principle and intent scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(d) is intended as additional scrutiny to prevent evergreening of chemical compounds and to provide fair competition rather than allowing minor modifications to extend monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts are alert to attempts to extend patent term by claiming trivial modifications; applicants should be prepared to show substantive, demonstrated improvements in therapeutic efficacy (for pharma) or genuine technical advances for other fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution strategy—what to include in replies
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a Section 3(d) objection, applicants should assess novelty status and, if necessary, present arguments on novelty/inventive step and present technical effects/advantages shown by the claimed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim falls within Section 3(d) categories, produce experimental/comparative data that directly demonstrate enhanced efficacy (therapeutic effect for drugs). If novelty can be established, argue that the subject matter is not a 'known substance/process' and therefore outside Section 3(d). Tailor responses to emphasize functional improvements tied to the statutory test of efficacy.
